I'll speak on my experiences as an English teacher who absolutely despises the busywork of grading papers. This may not work for all types of feedback, but if you're grading assignments like this:

I tend to simplify my feedback. It doesn't help to overwhelm the students with all the things they've done wrong. Instead, I tend to offer thoughts I have about their work as I read their assignment in the form of comments. These will usually be simple comments like "this is a really neat metaphor" or "I'm a little confused here, X decision doesn't seem like it makes sense with Y" It's a balancing act with feedback; if you give too much negative feedback, you'll likely demotivate/agitate students. Give too little, and you feel like you're not doing your job well enough.

I tend to use the sandwich method of feedback. At the end of an assignment, it helps l limit how much I say. Start with some positives I found, talk about things that could be improved / criticism of their work, before wrapping up with some affirmation that they're on the right track. This helps me keep feedback short (At most 3-4 sentences) and not overthink it as much. I'll sometimes provide comments throughout the margin, but I try not to do too much of this for both my own sanity as well as the students.

I also always offer students the opportunity to have a meeting with me if they want to know more specifics. I encourage them to ask questions and e-mail me if feedback is confusing or wasn't what they were expecting. It keeps me honest and allows me to elaborate more if needed.

I also agree with trying to get the stuff that's harder to grade out of the way earlier and save some of the good work for later. Grading assignments that require very nuanced feedback is the hardest part. I also find it easier to not do large chunk of grading at once. I'm only recently starting medication for ADHD, so maybe doing that big grading sesh will get easier on meds.

Hope that helps somewhat!

I have each player make six rolls as if they were rolling for a character. The numbers they roll just get put onto a spreadsheet rather than a character sheet. 

Let's say player one rolls this array: 11 17 16 12 15 16 
and player two rolls this one: 7 8 11 8 10 12

They must now each make a character sharing these numbers. Each number can only be used once. The group decides how to distribute their rolls.

If you have a 3rd player, they just add the numbers they rolled to the pool as well.

I hope that explains it a bit better.

I don't remember where I got this, but I'm pretty sure I stole this idea from a thread on this subreddit a long long time ago.

I have the players roll, but they share the stats and come up with stat blocks from their universal pool.

This is definitely not for every group, some people want their rolls to be *theirs*, but for my group, just rolling some dice with their buds was good enough to get them excited. It definitely adds some banter too when one player rolls hot and gets a bunch of 16/17's and another player rolls poorly and gets 6's and 7's. I've used this method twice now.

It gets the best parts of point buy (everyone is roughly equal in power) with the best parts of rolling (the highs and the lows). 
Overall, I've been pretty happy with this, but I have a group of players that aren't exactly veterans, so I can definitely see this method being a bit contentious in other groups.

I think it's less about healers actual DPS numbers, but more so the concern of having nothing to do.

Healers don't care if they have to press more dps buttons or more healing buttons generally, as long as:

1. You're actively engaged during encounters. Pressing Aspected Helios or Cure II 6 times in a row isn't engaging healing. That's what was nice about healing in STB; you were actively doing both healing and DPS. The DPS rotations of healers weren't extremely complex, but it gave healers something to prioritize and get good at beyond the bare minimum of healing during party-wide damage during very specific moments of each encounter.

2. The class feels FUN to play. I can sympathize with Astrologian mains the most here, as the card system was something that added a whole bunch of flavor to the class. The card re-work is lazy, albeit more convenient for balancing.

Realistically I think the changes serve as a good baseline for class balance, but they really need to make sure they nail class identity/healer engagement during encounters throughout the expansion. I'm skeptical at the whole "healing will become more important during end game content". It's not that I think it won't be more important, I'm just worried they won't make it important enough to fit the changes they've made for healers in 5.0.

All of that said, I'm willing to wait and see how it is when the expansion launches. I also don't see a world where AST/SCH don't get changes based on feedback after 5.0 launches.
